title: Can you really do two things at once?
hook: Multitasking feels efficient, but every switch has a price.
summary: Mostly not: in experiments, every switch between tasks costs time, and the cost grows with harder tasks.

cardBlocks.text: In a 2001 study, researchers from the University of Michigan and the US Federal Aviation Administration had young adults switch between tasks, such as solving math problems and classifying geometric shapes. For every type of task, people lost time whenever they switched, and they lost more when the tasks were complex or unfamiliar.

Each switch costs only several tenths of a second, but that adds up when people go back and forth many times. The volunteers were also slower and did the tasks worse, even when offered cash for good work. Multitasking may feel efficient, but it can end up taking longer.
Every task switch costs time; added up, switching makes multitasking slower and less accurate.

deepDiveBlocks.text: The researchers suggested that the brain’s executive control works in two stages: goal shifting ("I want to do this now instead of that") and rule activation ("I’m turning off the rules for that and turning on the rules for this").
Even when the switch is predictable

In 1995, Robert Rogers and Stephen Monsell had people do two trials of one task, then two of another, so every switch came at a predictable moment. Even so, people slowed down right after each switch.

Meyer points out that half a second lost to a task switch can make a life-or-death difference for a driver on a phone: in that time, the car can travel far enough to hit an obstacle that could otherwise have been avoided.

claims.text: In a 2001 study, researchers from the University of Michigan and the US Federal Aviation Administration had young adults switch between tasks such as math problems and classifying geometric shapes.

support.excerpt: Joshua Rubinstein, Ph.D., of the Federal Aviation Administration, and David Meyer, Ph.D., and Jeffrey Evans, Ph.D., both at the University of Michigan
young adult subjects (in turn, 12, 36, 36 and 24 in number) switched between different tasks, such as solving math problems or classifying geometric objects.

claims.text: For every type of task, people lost time when they switched, and lost more with more complex tasks.

support.excerpt: for all types of tasks, subjects lost time when they had to switch from one task to another, and time costs increased with the complexity of the tasks

claims.text: Switching cost more time when the new task was less familiar.

support.excerpt: Time costs also were greater when subjects switched to tasks that were relatively unfamiliar.

claims.text: Each switch costs several tenths of a second, which adds up when people switch back and forth repeatedly.

support.excerpt: Rule activation itself takes significant amounts of time, several tenths of a second -- which can add up when people switch back and forth repeatedly between tasks.

claims.text: When switching, people were slower and less accurate; in the 2001 study this held even when they were offered cash for good work.

support.excerpt: The volunteers accomplished the tasks more slowly and did them more poorly, even when offered cash for jobs well done.
This disruption is characterized by a slower performance and decrease in accuracy

claims.text: Multitasking may seem efficient but can take more time in the end.

support.excerpt: Thus, multitasking may seem more efficient on the surface, but may actually take more time in the end.

claims.text: The researchers suggested that executive control has two stages: goal shifting and rule activation.

support.excerpt: The researchers say their results suggest that executive control involves two distinct, complementary stages: goal shifting ("I want to do this now instead of that") and rule activation ("I'm turning off the rules for that and turning on the rules for this").

claims.text: In 1995, Rogers and Monsell had people switch tasks every two trials, a predictable switch, and people still slowed down right after each switch.

support.excerpt: Robert Rogers' and Stephen Monsell’s 1995 paper

In this task, participants carry out two trials of task A, followed by two trails of task B, and then back to task A. Hence, a task switch occurs every two trials. The difficulty to switch between tasks is expressed as the slow down immediately following a task switch.
The cost of a predictable switch between simple cognitive tasks

claims.text: According to Meyer, half a second lost to a task switch can be the difference between life and death for a driver on a phone, because the car can travel far enough to hit an obstacle.

support.excerpt: Meyer points out, a mere half second of time lost to task switching can mean the difference between life and death for a driver using a cell phone, because during the time that the car is not totally under control, it can travel far enough to crash into obstacles the driver might have otherwise avoided.
